---
title: "What is a package manager?"
---

A **package manager** is software that installs, updates, removes, and keeps track of other software packages, together with the constraints between them. Operating systems have long had their own (`apt` on Debian/Ubuntu, `brew` on macOS, `winget` on Windows); Python has its own ecosystem, built around the [Python Package Index (PyPI)](https://pypi.org/) as the central public repository.

In Python, a *package* is simply reusable code, published so that other people do not need to write it themselves. For example:

- `pandas` provides data structures and operations for tabular data;
- `numpy` provides fast, array-based numerical computing;
- `scikit-learn` provides general-purpose machine-learning algorithms;
- `jupyterlab` provides an interactive, notebook-based interface to Python.

### Dependencies, and why resolution is hard

A package can itself depend on other packages, which depend on others in turn. These indirect requirements are called **transitive dependencies**. Installing `pandas`, for example, pulls in `numpy` as a dependency without you asking for `numpy` by name.

This quickly produces a *dependency graph* rather than a simple list. Two direct dependencies you ask for might each place different, incompatible constraints on a shared transitive dependency — package A might require `numpy>=1.24`, while package B only supports `numpy<1.24`. Finding a single set of versions that satisfies every constraint simultaneously is known as **dependency resolution**, and in general it is a computationally hard problem (it is closely related to the Boolean satisfiability problem, SAT). This is precisely the part of environment management that is tedious and error-prone to do by hand, and precisely the part a package manager exists to automate.

Historically, Python's own installer, `pip`, resolved dependencies using a comparatively simple, backtracking algorithm, and for a long time did not resolve them at all — it simply installed packages in the order given, sometimes silently overwriting an already-installed, compatible version with an incompatible one. This is one of the main reasons the community has since built more sophisticated tools (`pip-tools`, `Poetry`, `PDM`, `conda`, and now `uv`) around a proper resolver.

### Why use `uv`?

[`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), developed by Astral, is deliberately scoped to do more than resolve and install packages. It also:

- installs and manages **Python interpreters themselves** (not just packages);
- creates and manages per-project **virtual environments** automatically;
- adds and removes a project's declared dependencies;
- resolves a consistent, compatible set of versions for the full dependency graph;
- writes a **lockfile** recording exactly which versions were resolved;
- runs commands inside the correct project environment on request.

Two practical reasons make `uv` a good default choice for a short teaching session and for everyday research use. First, it is implemented in Rust and is substantially faster than the pure-Python tools it replaces, particularly for dependency resolution and installation — for a live demonstration, this means we are not sitting waiting for a spinner. Second, it deliberately unifies steps that other tools historically required several separate programs for (interpreter installation, environment creation, dependency locking), which reduces the number of moving parts a beginner needs to hold in their head at once.

::: {.callout-note}
### `uv` is not the only viable option

`conda`/`mamba` remain the standard choice when a project's dependencies include non-Python components (compiled libraries, R packages, and so on) that PyPI does not distribute.

`Poetry` and `PDM` offer broadly similar project-based workflows to `uv`. The concepts in this session — declared dependencies, a resolved lockfile, and an isolated environment reconstructable from both — apply to all of them; only the specific commands differ.
:::
